title: Three watches (Berakhot 3a)
hookLine: the night has three watches, and in each the Talmud pictures God grieving for the exile
tomorrow: how did King David know when it was midnight?

cards: Two in the morning, phone face down, and the house makes its night sounds: the fridge, a dog somewhere, a car going by. Berakhot's next page divides the night exactly that way, by what you hear.
And it says that in every part of the night, someone else is awake too.

teach.b: The night has three watches, says Rabbi Eliezer, and each has a sign. In the first, the donkey brays. In the second, dogs bark.
In the third, a baby nurses at its mother's breast, and a wife talks quietly with her husband. You can tell the hour by ear. Then the page adds something startling.

teach.h: GOD ROARS LIKE A LION, GRIEVING.
teach.b: In the name of Rav it says: in each watch, God sits and roars like a lion, grieving. Woe to the children, for whose sake I destroyed My house, burned My Temple, and sent them into exile among the nations.
The verse behind it is from Jeremiah: the LORD roars from on high. So in this picture, God is the one awake at two in the morning, missing children who are far away. Not a judge on a bench.
A parent at the window. The same page doesn't leave it there.

teach.h: MAY HIS GREAT NAME BE BLESSED.
teach.b: When people gather in their synagogues and study halls and answer, may His great name be blessed, God shakes His head and says: happy is the king who is praised like this in his house. Grief and comfort, side by side.
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud tells time by a donkey, a dog and a baby, and then says God keeps those watches too.
So being awake in the night, thinking of someone far away, isn't only a failure to sleep. On this page, it's what God does.

how: Many Jews say the bedtime Shema before sleep, and some keep a custom called Tikkun Chatzot, rising around midnight to mourn the destruction of the Temple.

o: the three parts of the night, each with its own sign
three short prayers said before going to sleep
three guards posted at the Temple gates at night

games.q: the three watches — tap the pairs.
p: a baby nurses; a couple talks
God roars like a lion, grieving

s: the Talmud tells the night's watches by the stars
by ear: a donkey brays, dogs bark, a baby nurses.
in Berakhot 3a, God is pictured grieving in each watch of the night
in Rav's name: God roars like a lion over the children sent into exile.
the page ends on grief and nothing else
it adds comfort: when people answer 'may His great name be blessed', God says happy is the king praised like this.

games.q: a friend's grandmother moved across the country, and your friend feels silly lying awake missing her. what does this page offer?
o: missing someone in the night is something the Talmud pictures God doing too.
the watches are a reminder to sleep through the night and let it go.
the third watch is for talking, so she should call her grandmother then.
games.why: Berakhot 3a pictures God awake in every watch, grieving for children far away. the page doesn't call that weakness; it calls it love.

practice: Bring to mind one person who's far away tonight, across town or across an ocean. Picture the hour where they are and what they might be hearing: a dog, traffic, a kettle. Keep them company in your mind for the whole sit.

wordCard.voice: Three watches. The Talmud's night, told by ear: a donkey, dogs, a baby. And in each one, God awake, missing the children.

orig.note: Hebrew: watches, the parts of the night; Rabbi Eliezer counts three.

carryVoice: Keep this close: three watches, and in every one, someone else is awake. Berakhot, day two.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 3a (three watches and their signs; God roars like a lion in each watch, in Rav's name; 'happy is the king who is praised like this in his house')
Jeremiah 25:30 (the LORD roars from on high)
